definition: Praising or flattering so heavily that it seems excessive or insincere.
example: Her fulsome thank-you note gushed so much that it read almost like sarcasm.
nuance: Effusive praise can be sincere, but fulsome praise traditionally sounds false from excess. The word does not simply mean full or plentiful.
prompt: A salesperson greets a customer who is browsing for a new sofa.
options: His fulsome praise of my taste felt like a sales tactic.
The fulsome sofa had cushions stuffed so thick they barely fit the frame.
His fulsome silence let me wander the showroom without any pressure at all.
His fulsome criticism of every sofa I touched made me want to leave the store.
reasons: Gushing compliments that seem calculated are exactly the overdone flattery the word describes.
This confuses the word with full or overstuffed; it describes praise or manner, not padding.
Saying nothing offers no flattery, so there is nothing excessive to describe.
Constant fault-finding is the reverse of laying on compliments too thickly.

practice.prompt: A student introduces a visiting author before a school assembly.
options: The fulsome introduction called her a genius so often that she squirmed.
The fulsome introduction was so curt that the author had barely stood before it ended.
The fulsome auditorium had no empty seats, so latecomers waited in the hall.
The fulsome introduction listed only the years her books came out, offering no opinion.
reasons: Repeated, heavy-handed praise that embarrasses the guest shows flattery gone too far.
A short, restrained introduction lacks the excess the word requires.
This mistakes the word for crowded or full; it has nothing to do with capacity.
A neutral list of dates contains no praise, let alone too much of it.
